description: Knechtle argues that Christianity better explains costly out-group concern, sacrificial love, and enduring hope than an evolutionary picture he portrays as naturally violent.
critique: Strongest feature: Knechtle identifies sympathy, sacrificial love, aid to outsiders, and persistent hope, giving this experiential-fit case constructive responsiveness and substantial motion relevance without replying to opposition. Principal limitation: His excerpt asserts Judeo-Christian cultural causation and portrays evolution as naturally violent, offering neither historical corroboration nor engagement with evolutionary cooperation, while leaving hope's connection to eternal reality underdetermined. Live burden: He must show that costly out-group concern resists natural explanation, distinguish Christianity's superiority from cultural influence or psychological usefulness, and justify why durable hope indicates a specifically Christian eternal reality. Locked score: The 59 reflects the frozen unevenness: strong relevance and constructive contact sustain the argument, but thin evidence, incomplete comparison, imprecise causation, and an uncharitable evolutionary contrast substantially restrain its force.
